title: Browsers, servers, and requests
goals: Describe the path from typing a URL to seeing a page
Distinguish browser, DNS, and web server roles
Read a simple HTTP status code
bodyMd:
## What happens when you hit Enter?

When you type `https://doyintech.vercel.app` and press Enter, your computer does not magically "know" the page. It follows a pipeline:

1. **DNS** — resolve the host name to an IP address.
2. **TCP/TLS** — open a secure connection to that IP.
3. **HTTP request** — ask for a specific resource (`GET /`).
4. **Server response** — HTML (and later CSS/JS) comes back with a **status code**.
5. **Render** — the browser turns markup into pixels.

### Status codes you will see often

| Code | Meaning |
|------|--------|
| 200 | OK — body is the resource |
| 301 / 302 | Redirect — go somewhere else |
| 404 | Not found |
| 500 | Server error |

### Why this matters for developers

Every bug that looks like "the page is blank" is somewhere in this chain: wrong URL, DNS, TLS, status code, or the HTML itself. Learning the chain makes debugging predictable.

codeBlocks.title: Inspect response headers
codeBlocks.code:
curl -I https://example.com
# Look for: HTTP/2 200, content-type, server

practice.prompt: Run `curl -I` against any public site. Write down the status line and content-type.
practice.solution: You should see a line like HTTP/2 200 and a content-type such as text/html.

quiz.question: What does DNS primarily do?
choices: Map a host name to an IP address
quiz.explain: DNS is the phone book of the internet: names → addresses.

quiz.question: A 404 status means:
choices: The resource was not found at that path
quiz.explain: 404 is "not found" for that URL path — the server itself may still be healthy.

video.script: Welcome to Web Foundations. In the next few minutes we will walk the exact path your browser takes when you open a website — from the address bar, through DNS, to the HTML that lands on your screen. No mysticism: just a clear request and response. By the end you will be able to explain a 200, a 404, and why curl is a developer's flashlight.
